analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, erasing federal air pollution controls added that year.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, introduced by Rep. Tom DeLay with 2 cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments set national rules that cut acid rain, required cleaner gasoline, tightened smog and soot limits, and forced reductions in toxic air pollution from factories. This bill would have erased all of those requirements in one sentence, returning the country to the weaker air rules of the 1970s. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its subcommittees, but was never scheduled for any hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been coal-burning power plants, oil refineries, chemical plants, and other large polluters. The 1990 amendments required utilities to cut sulfur dioxide emissions (the main cause of acid rain), set tighter urban air quality deadlines, and imposed controls on 189 toxic air pollutants. Repeal would have removed those obligations and their compliance costs, shifting the cost onto the public as dirtier air, acid rain damage, and higher health costs.

how_it_helps.text: Repealing Public Law 101-549 would have eliminated the acid rain program that required power plants to cut sulfur dioxide emissions, and removed requirements for cleaner fuels, stricter smog standards, and controls on toxic air emissions from industrial sources [S2][S3].
It would have ended the compliance obligations and costs the 1990 amendments placed on utilities, refineries, and chemical and manufacturing plants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people would have paid through dirtier air: more acid rain damaging lakes, forests, and buildings; more smog and soot aggravating asthma and heart and lung disease; and uncontrolled emissions of toxic chemicals near factories. Local governments and states would also have lost the federal framework they rely on to set and enforce air quality standards.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have stripped away acid rain controls, urban smog deadlines, and limits on 189 toxic air pollutants, with the health burden falling on people living near highways, power plants, and industrial facilities [S2][S3].

Repealing a statute wholesale, rather than revising specific rules, would have removed even provisions most users of the law accepted, and would have thrown existing state and industry compliance programs into legal uncertainty, since the underlying 1970-era Clean Air Act did not contain the 1990 requirements [S3].

Supporters' good-faith argument was that the 1990 amendments imposed large compliance costs on utilities and manufacturers; the bill addressed that concern, but only by eliminating the pollution protections entirely rather than targeting costs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a single sentence of repeal with no replacement framework. Whatever compliance costs the 1990 amendments imposed on industry, erasing acid rain controls, smog standards, and toxic emissions limits in their entirety would have traded those costs for measurably dirtier air and the health problems that follow. The bill addressed industry cost concerns only at the price of removing every public health protection added in 1990, with nothing put in their place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 1995 and sent to the House Commerce Committee and two of its subcommittees, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay (R-TX) introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, at the start of the new Republican majority [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce on January 11, 1995 [S1][S5].
On February 6, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it sat without further action [S5].
Only two Republican members cosponsored the bill, and no further action of any kind appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the acid rain program, cleaner fuels, smog limits, and toxic air pollution controls of the 1990 amendments, because the repeal never advanced. The industries that would have shed compliance costs never gained them, and the committee leadership that never scheduled action faced no political cost for letting the bill expire.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill had no Democratic cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists, but support came entirely from one party.

industries.note: The 1990 amendments created the acid rain program requiring utilities to cut sulfur dioxide emissions; repeal would have removed those obligations and their compliance costs, leaving the public to bear the resulting pollution.

The 1990 amendments required cleaner-burning gasoline and tighter fuel standards; repeal would have ended those requirements, saving refiners money while increasing smog and air toxics for the public.

The amendments set technology-based limits on emissions of 189 toxic air pollutants from industrial sources; repeal would have freed these plants from those controls at the expense of air quality in nearby communities.
